1-2: A time some hours or minutes later or earlier: when something ends from its start, or starts from its end.
How long something lasts, from its start and its end: in hours or in minutes, or which of two lasts longer.
Sleep across midnight: from a time in the evening to a time in the morning.
A clock that strikes the hours: how many strokes in a few hours.
Two activities one after another, with a break between them.
A watch that is fast or slow by some minutes: the real time from what it shows.
Things done at the same time take no longer: three eggs boiled together in one pot.
Half past, quarter past and quarter to: times said in words, and the minutes in parts of an hour.
A clock face shows every time twice a day: how many times a day it shows a given hour.
A bus that leaves every few minutes: the next one after a given time.
Reading a clock face: the long hand counts five minutes for each number, and the short hand, standing between two numbers, gives the earlier one as the hour.
The hours of a day shared out, such as sleep, school and play: together they make twenty-four, so one part is what the others leave of the day.
An alarm clock with a twelve-hour face, set in the evening for a morning hour: it rings the next time its hands reach that hour, which may be the same evening.
3-4: The minutes gone since one hour and those left until the next, one a given number of times the other: sixty minutes shared in that ratio give the time.
Minutes in a few hours and a half.
A length of time that grows by the same few minutes every day, such as daylight in spring: its length some days later, sixty minutes making an hour.
Jobs with room for only a few at a time, such as frying three pancakes two at a time, a minute a side: with more pancakes than places, the least time leaves no place empty while a side waits.
A clock face seen in a mirror: left and right swap, so the time it seems to show and the real time add up to twelve hours, twelve o'clock counting as nought.
A trip with a change, read from two timetables: the latest first bus that still catches the train, and the wait at the change.
A digital clock over a day: how many times it shows a pattern, such as four equal digits.
The middle of a stretch of time, such as halfway between sunrise and sunset: half its length added to its start.
The 24-hour clock and the 12-hour clock: the same moment written both ways.
Minutes and seconds: the times of runners in a race, compared or added.
5-6: Night trips and shifts across midnight: how long one lasts with its breaks, or which of two is longer.
Phoning between time zones: the time at the other end.
A flight across time zones: the local times of take-off and landing.
The hands of a clock on top of each other: how many times in a day, and why not 24.
Two buses on one route, one every 12 minutes and one every 18: when they next leave together.
A film shown twice with a break between: when the second showing ends.
A flight there and back: the time in the air and the difference between the zones.
A watch that gains a few minutes each hour: the true time when it shows a given time.
Two clocks, one gaining and one losing: when they show the same time again.
The angle between the hands of a clock at a given time.
Clocks each wrong by a known number of minutes, without saying whether fast or slow: the true time is the one each reading misses by exactly its own error.
Boats that leave both ends of a route at the same hour every day, each so many days on the way: one meets those sailing when it starts and those leaving before it arrives.
Someone met on the way by a car that turns back at once and gets home some minutes early: the car skipped the drive there and back over the rest, half those minutes each way.
Moments when a 24-hour digital clock shows as many minutes as hours, such as 07:07: within a day each comes an hour and a minute after the one before.
